For a harmonic oscillator, the vibrational energies are
\[
E_\nu=\hbar\omega\left(\nu+\frac{1}{2}\right),
\qquad
\omega=\sqrt{\frac{k}{\mu}}.
\]

title: 13  BCH expansion and exponentials of operators
text:
13.1 Introduction
Coupled-cluster calculations use exponentials of operators. We will treat the operators as finite square matrices. For a square matrix \(T\), define the matrix exponential by the power series
\[
\exp(T) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{T^n}{n!}.
\tag{13.1}\]
The zeroth power is the identity matrix, \(T^0=I\).
crumbs: 13  BCH expansion and exponentials of operators

title: 13  BCH expansion and exponentials of operators
text:
13.2 Exercises

Exercise 13.1 Consider the matrix exponential in Equation 13.1.

Write the first five terms of the power series.
Explain why \(T\) must be square for every term in the series to be defined.
Let
\[
T =
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 1 \\
-1 & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Compute \(T^2\), \(T^3\), and \(T^4\). Use the results to evaluate the degree-four approximation to \(\exp(T)\).
crumbs: 13  BCH expansion and exponentials of operators

title: 13  BCH expansion and exponentials of operators
text:
13.3 Solutions

13.3.1 Solution to Exercise 13.1

Substituting \(n=0,1,2,3,4\) in Equation 13.1 gives
\[
\exp(T)
= I + T + \frac{1}{2}T^2 + \frac{1}{6}T^3
+ \frac{1}{24}T^4 + \cdots.
\]
The product \(T^2=TT\) requires the number of columns of the first factor to equal the number of rows of the second. Repeated powers \(T^n\) therefore keep the same dimensions only when \(T\) is square. The identity \(I=T^0\) must have those dimensions as well.
Direct multiplication gives
\[
T^2=-I, \qquad T^3=-T, \qquad T^4=I.
\]
The degree-four approximation is
\[
\begin{aligned}
I + T + \frac{1}{2}T^2 + \frac{1}{6}T^3 + \frac{1}{24}T^4
&= I + T - \frac{1}{2}I - \frac{1}{6}T + \frac{1}{24}I \\
&= \frac{13}{24}I + \frac{5}{6}T \\
&=
\begin{bmatrix}
13/24 & 5/6 \\
-5/6 & 13/24
\end{bmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
\]
